newsitem.title: USA: U.S. durable goods orders drop sharply in March.
newsitem.headline: U.S. durable goods orders drop sharply in March.

text.p: Orders for costly manufactured goods were broadly lower in March, the Commerce Department said on Tuesday, dropping at the sharpest rate in seven months.

New orders for durable goods fell 3 percent last month to a seasonally adjusted $171.5 billion. It was the biggest monthly plunge since a 3.6 percent decrease in orders last August and a much weaker performance than anticipated by Wall Street economists, who had forecast no change from February's revised 0.8 percent gain.
Every major category of manufactured product showed weaker orders in March than in February. In addition, order backlogs fell for the first time since August.
Previously, the department estimated February durables orders had risen by 1.5 percent but it cut that back to a revised 0.8 percent gain.

Orders for durable goods -- relatively costly items like cars and home appliances that are intended to last at least three years -- are taken as an indicator of the manufacturing sector's vigour, which in turn weighs heavily on the overall economy.

Transportation orders fell 4.3 percent in March to a seasonally adjusted $37.5 billion after a 7.3 percent decline in February. The department said that orders fell for both new aircraft and parts and for new cars and parts.
Transportation is the largest single category of durable goods, accounting for more than one-fifth of the monthly value of manufactured goods.
Excluding transportation, durables orders fell 2.6 percent in March -- the biggest drop since a 3 percent decrease in June 1991 -- after rising 3.4 percent in February.

The biggest percentage decline occurred in orders for electronic and electrical equipment, down 5.9 percent to $28.8 billion following a 7.7 percent increase in February. The Commerce Department said orders were softer for communications equipment and for electronic components.
Industrial machinery and equipment orders fell 1.2 percent to $32.8 billion after a 2.1 percent pickup in February.
Primary metals orders declined for a second straight month, falling 0.6 percent to $15.7 billion following a 0.7 percent fall in February.

Orders for defence goods, which experience wide monthly swings, plummeted 16.8 percent last month to $4.5 billion after a 12.4 percent drop in February. If defence is excluded, overall orders in March were down 2.6 percent after gaining 1.3 percent in February.
Orders for non-defence capital goods, an indication of business investment in new equipment, were off by 4.4 percent last month to $44.8 billion after increasing 2.3 percent in February.
Shipments of durable goods, an indication of current demand, rose 0.7 percent to $174.9 billion in March after rising 1.9 percent in February.
Unfilled orders declined 0.7 percent to $493.8 billion in March -- the first drop in order backlogs since August -- after a 0.6 percent gain in February.
